n: The Shunammite woman from chapter 4 reappears. Elisha had warned her of a coming seven-year famine and told her to live abroad wherever she could. The episode probably happened earlier than the events of chapter 7.

f.w: whose son he had restored to life

n: She trusted the prophet’s word and moved with her household to Philistine territory for seven years.
When she returned, her property had been taken over—perhaps by the crown or by squatters—so she went to appeal to the king.

f.g: make a legal appeal to the king.

n: At that very moment, the king is asking Gehazi to tell him Elisha’s great works.
Just as Gehazi tells of the boy raised from death, the woman and her son walk in. The timing reveals God’s quiet providence.
She confirms the story, and the king orders all her land restored, plus the income from its crops during her absence. The Lord cares for the faithful even through ordinary legal matters.

f.g: the harvest income from her land.

n: Elisha travels to Damascus, Aram’s capital. Ben-hadad is sick and hears that the famous man of God has arrived.
Ben-hadad tells his officer Hazael to bring a gift and ask the Lord, through Elisha, whether he will recover. The enemy king now seeks Israel’s God.

f.g: ‘God has seen’; an Aramean official, later king.

n: Hazael comes with forty camel-loads of Damascus’s finest goods and calls Ben-hadad “your son”—respectful language for a prophet.
Elisha’s answer is two-sided: the illness itself would not kill Ben-hadad, but the Lord has shown that he will die anyway.
Elisha stares at Hazael until Hazael is embarrassed—then the prophet weeps. He sees what is in Hazael’s heart.
Elisha explains: he foresees the terrible war crimes Hazael will commit against Israel. A prophet’s gift can be a heavy burden.

f.w: the evil that thou wilt do

n: Hazael protests, “Am I a dog to do such a thing?”—yet Elisha reveals that he will become king of Aram, fulfilling the commission given to Elijah at Horeb.

f.w: thou shalt be king over Syria

n: Hazael tells Ben-hadad only half the message: he will recover.
The next day Hazael smothers the king with a wet cloth and takes the throne. An Assyrian inscription calls Hazael “the son of a nobody,” meaning a usurper.
The narrative turns to Judah. Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat becomes king, sharing the throne with his father for a time. Two kings named Jehoram/Joram now rule at once in Israel and Judah.
He was thirty-two and reigned eight years (about 848–841 BC as sole king).
He married Athaliah, Ahab and Jezebel’s daughter, and followed their ways. Jehoshaphat’s alliance with Ahab’s family now brings Baal worship into Judah.

f.w: the daughter of Ahab was his wife

n: Despite Jehoram’s evil, the Lord preserved Judah for David’s sake, keeping the promise of an enduring “lamp.”
Edom, long under Judah’s control, revolted and crowned its own king—fulfilling Isaac’s blessing that Esau would one day break Jacob’s yoke.
Jehoram marched to Zair with his chariots. Surrounded by night, he broke through, but his army fled home.

f.g: an unknown location, probably near Edom.

n: Edom stayed independent, and Libnah, a town on Judah’s western border, also rebelled—signs of a weakening kingdom.

f.g: a town in the lowlands of Judah near Philistia.

n: Joram’s acts are in Judah’s chronicles. Chronicles adds that he died of a painful disease and was not mourned.

f.w: the rest of the acts of Joram

n: He dies and his son Ahaziah succeeds him.
Ahaziah becomes king of Judah in the twelfth year of Joram of Israel. (Israel’s former king Ahaziah was a different man.)
He was twenty-two and reigned only one year. His mother Athaliah is called the “daughter” (granddaughter) of Omri.

f.g: ‘Jehovah is exalted’; daughter of Ahab and Jezebel.

n: Related by marriage to Ahab’s house, he followed its idolatry.
Ahaziah joins his uncle Joram of Israel in war against Hazael at Ramoth-gilead—the same city where Ahab had died. Joram is wounded.
Joram goes to Jezreel to recover, and Ahaziah visits him there. Both kings in one place sets the stage for Jehu’s coup in the next chapter.
